supremeCourt.name: Corte Suprema de Justicia de la Nación
supremeCourt.appointmentMethod: Nominated by the President, confirmed by 2/3 of the Senate.
supremeCourt.fspEraChanges: In 1990 President Menem (Peronist, pre-Kirchner) expanded the court from 5 to 9 (Law 23.774), creating an "automatic majority". In 2006 the Kirchnerist government reduced it back to 5 (Law 26.183) and had tightened the appointment process (Decree 222/03, 2003). So the packing predates the Kirchnerist (FSP-affiliated) governments, which actually de-packed it — a useful counter to a simplistic 'FSP packs courts' reading.
supremeCourt.stillServing: After the retirements of Highton (2021) and Maqueda (2024), the court fell below its 5-seat complement to 3 justices; President Milei's attempts to fill the seats by decree (Lijo, García-Mansilla) failed in the Senate (2025), leaving a deadlock as of 2026.

courtHistory.event: Earlier history: the Corte Suprema was installed in 1863 (5 justices). In 1947 Perón's Congress removed 4 of the 5 justices; the court was expanded 5→7 (1958) and returned to 5 (1966); the 1976–83 junta replaced it. Reshaping the court by incoming governments was a long-running pattern before 1990.
Law 23.774 (Menem) expanded the court from 5 to 9, creating the 'automatic majority'.
Decree 222/03 (Néstor Kirchner) opened Supreme Court nominations to public scrutiny, applied to the post-Menem vacancies.
Law 26.183 (promoted by Cristina Fernández de Kirchner) reduced the court from 9 back to 5, reversing Menem's expansion.

After Highton (2021) and Maqueda (2024) left, the court fell to 3 justices; Milei's decree appointments (Lijo, García-Mansilla) were rejected by the Senate in 2025, leaving the seats vacant amid a deadlock.
